section.heading: 4.4 Coordinate Systems
section.paragraph: An important reason for specifying a basis $$B$$ for a vector space $$V$$ is to impose a “coordinate system” on $$V$$ . This section will show that if $$B$$ contains $$n$$ vectors, then the coordinate system will make $$V$$ act like $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . If $$V$$ is already $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ itself, then $$B$$ will determine a coordinate system that gives a new “view” of $$V$$ .
The existence of coordinate systems rests on the following fundamental result.

note.title: Theorem 8
note.heading: Theorem 8
The Unique Representation Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1},\ldots\mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ be a basis for a vector space $$V$$ . Then for each $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$V$$ , there exists a unique set of scalars $$c_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} c_{n}$$ such that

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Since $$B$$ spans $$V$$ , there exist scalars such that (1) holds. Suppose $$\mathbf{x}$$ also has the representation
$$\mathbf{x} = d_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + d_{n} \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
for scalars $$d_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} d_{n}$$ . Then, subtracting, we have
$$0 = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x} = \left(\right. c_{1} - d_{1} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + \left(\right. c_{n} - d_{n} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
Since $$B$$ is linearly independent, the weights in (2) must all be zero. That is, $$c_{j} = d_{j}$$ for $$1 \leq j \leq n$$ .

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Suppose $$B = \text{\{} \mathbf{b}_{1} \text{,…} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{n} \text{\}}$$ is a basis for a vector space $$V$$ and $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$V$$ . The coordinates of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to the basis $$B$$ (or the $$\mathbf{\mathit{B}} -\textbf{coordinates}$$ of $$\mathbf{x}$$ ) are the weights $$c_{1} \text{,…,} c_{n}$$ such that $$\mathbf{x} = c_{1}\mathbf{b}_{1} + \cdots + c_{n}\mathbf{b}_{n}$$ .

section.paragraph: If $$c_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} c_{n}$$ are the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of $$\mathbf{x}$$ , then the vector in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$
$$\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} \end{bmatrix}_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ \vdots \\ c_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$

is the coordinate vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ (relative to B), or the $$\mathbf{B}\textbf{-coordinate} \mathbf{vector}$$ of x. The mapping $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x} \end{bmatrix}_{B}$$ is the coordinate mapping (determined by $$\mathbf{B}$$ ﻿).1

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Consider a basis $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{2} \right\}$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ , where $$\mathbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Suppose an $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ has the coordinate vector $$[\mathbf{x}_{B}] = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find $$\mathbf{x}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The $$B$$ -coordinates of $$\mathbf{x}$$ tell how to build $$\mathbf{x}$$ from the vectors in $$B$$ . That is,
$$\mathbf{x} = ( - 2 ) \mathbf{b}_{1} + 3 \mathbf{b}_{2} = ( - 2 ) \left[\right. 1 0 \left]\right. + \text{3} \left[\right. 1 2 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 1 6 \left]\right.$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: The entries in the vector $$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ are the coordinates of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to the standard basis $$\varepsilon = \left\{ \mathbf{e}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{e}_{2} \right\}$$ , since
$$\left[\right. 1 6 \left]\right. = 1 \left[\right. 1 0 \left]\right. + 6 \left[\right. 0 1 \left]\right. = 1 \mathbf{e}_{1} + 6 \mathbf{e}_{2}$$
If $$\varepsilon = \left\{ \mathbf{e}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{e}_{2} \right\}$$ , then $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{\varepsilon} = \mathbf{x}$$ .

section.heading: A Graphical Interpretation of Coordinates
section.paragraph: A coordinate system on a set consists of a one-to-one mapping of the points in the set into $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . For example, ordinary graph paper provides a coordinate system for the plane when one selects perpendicular axes and a unit of measurement on each axis. Figure 1 shows the standard basis $$\left\{ \mathbf{e}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{e}_{2} \right\}$$ , the vectors $$\mathbf{b}_{1}( = \mathbf{e}_{1})$$ and $$\mathbf{b}_{2}$$ from Example 1, and the vector $$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}$$ . The coordinates $$1$$ and $$6$$ give the location of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to the standard basis: $$1$$ unit in the $$\mathbf{e}_{1}$$ direction and $$6$$ units in the $$\mathbf{e}_{2}$$ direction.

image.alt: A figure shows five closed points plotted on a standard graph paper.

section.paragraph: Figure 2 shows the vectors $$\mathbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\mathbf{x}$$ from Figure 1. (Geometrically, the three vectors lie on a vertical line in both figures.) However, the standard coordinate grid was erased and replaced by a grid especially adapted to the basis $$\lbrack B\rbrack$$ in Example 1. The coordinate vector $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ gives the location of $$\mathbf{x}$$ on this new coordinate system: $$- 2$$ units in the $$\mathbf{b}_{1}$$ direction and $$3$$ units in the $$\mathbf{b}_{2}$$ direction.

image.alt: A figure shows four closed points plotted on a beta graph paper.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: In crystallography, the description of a crystal lattice is aided by choosing a basis $$\{\mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{,} \mathbf{w}\}$$ for $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ that corresponds to three adjacent edges of one “unit cell” of the crystal. An entire lattice is constructed by stacking together many copies of one cell. There are fourteen basic types of unit cells; three are displayed in Figure 3.2

image.alt: Three types of crystal lattice: (a) Simple monoclinic, (b) Body-centered cubic, and (c) Face-centered orthorhombic.

example.paragraph: The coordinates of atoms within the crystal are given relative to the basis for the lattice. For instance,
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
identifies the top face-centered atom in the cell in Figure 3(c).

section.heading: Coordinates in ℝn
section.paragraph: When a basis $$B$$ for $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is fixed, the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of a specified $$\mathbf{x}$$ is easily found, as in the next example.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{b}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$x = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{2} \right\}$$ . Find the coordinate vector $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to $$B$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The $$B - \text{coordinates}$$ ﻿ $$c_{1} \text{,} c_{2}$$ of $$\mathbf{x}$$ satisfy
$$c_{1} \underset{\mathbf{b}_{1}}{\left[\right. 2 1 \left]\right.} + c_{2} \underset{\mathbf{b}_{2}}{\left[\right. - 1 1 \left]\right.} = \underset{\mathbf{x}}{\left[\right. 4 5 \left]\right.}$$
or

$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}b_{1}\end{matrix}\end{matrix} & b_{2} & & & & & x$$

This equation can be solved by row operations on an augmented matrix or by multiplying the vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ by the inverse of the matrix. In any case, the solution is $$c_{1} = 3$$ , $$c_{2} = 2$$ . Thus $$\mathbf{x} = 3\mathbf{b}_{1} + 2\mathbf{b}_{2}$$ , and
$$\left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. c_{1} c_{2} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 3 2 \left]\right.$$
See Figure 4.

image.alt: A graph shows a rectangle with one of its vertices at the origin.

figure.caption: Figure 4 The B-coordinate vector of x is (3, 2)

section.paragraph: The matrix in (3) changes the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of a vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ into the standard coordinates for $$\mathbf{x}$$ . An analogous change of coordinates can be carried out in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ for a basis $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1},\ldots, \mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ . Let
$$P_{B} = \left[\right. \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} & \hdots & \mathbf{b}_{n} \left]\right.$$
Then the vector equation
$$\mathbf{x} = c_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + c_{2} \mathbf{b}_{2} + \hdots + c_{n} \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
is equivalent to
(4) $$\boxed{\mathbf{x} = P_{B} \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{B}}$$

We call $$P_{B}$$ the change-of-coordinates matrix from $$B$$ to the standard basis in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Left-multiplication by $$P_{B}$$ transforms the coordinate vector $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ into $$\mathbf{x}$$ . The change-of-coordinates equation (4) is important and will be needed at several points in Chapters 5 and 7.

Since the columns of $$P_{B}$$ form a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , $$P_{B}$$ is invertible (by the Invertible Matrix Theorem). Left-multiplication by $$P_{B}^{- 1}$$ converts $$\mathbf{x}$$ into its $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector:
$$P_{B}^{- 1} \mathbf{x} = \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{x} \left]\right.\right)_{B}$$

The correspondence $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ , produced here by $$P_{B}^{- 1}$$ , is the coordinate mapping mentioned earlier. Since $$P_{B}^{- 1}$$ is an invertible matrix, the coordinate mapping is a one-to-one linear transformation from $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ onto $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , by the Invertible Matrix Theorem. (See also Theorem 12 in Section 1.9.) This property of the coordinate mapping is also true in a general vector space that has a basis, as we shall see.
section.heading: The Coordinate Mapping
section.paragraph: Choosing a basis $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ for a vector space $$V$$ introduces a coordinate system in $$V$$ . The coordinate mapping $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{\left\lbrack { x} \right\rbrack}_{B}$$ connects the possibly unfamiliar space $$V$$ to the familiar space $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . See Figure 5. Points in $$V$$ can now be identified by their new “names.”

image.alt: A figure shows a vector space mapped into a point on the three-dimensional coordinate plane.

figure.caption: Figure 5 The coordinate mapping from V onto ℝn﻿

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
note.paragraph: Let $$B = \left\{ \mathbf{b}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{b}_{n} \right\}$$ be a basis for a vector space $$V$$ . Then the coordinate mapping $$\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathbf{\left\lbrack { x} \right\rbrack}_{B}$$ is a one-to-one linear transformation from $$V$$ onto $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Take two typical vectors in $$V$$ , say,
$$\mathbf{u} = c_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \mathbf{b}_{n} \mathbf{w} = d_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + d_{n} \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
Then, using vector operations,
$$\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} = \left(\right. c_{1} + d_{1} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + \left(\right. c_{n} + d_{n} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
It follows that

$$\left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. c_{1} & + & d_{1} & \vdots & c_{n} & + & d_{n} \left]\right. = \left[\right. c_{1} \vdots c_{n} \left]\right. + \left[\right. d_{1} \vdots d_{n} \left]\right. = \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u} \left]\right.\right)_{B} + \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{w} \left]\right.\right)_{B}$$
So the coordinate mapping preserves addition. If $$r$$ is any scalar, then

$$r \mathbf{u} = r \left(\right. c_{1} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \mathbf{b}_{n} \left.\right) = \left(\right. r c_{1} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{1} + \hdots + \left(\right. r c_{n} \left.\right) \mathbf{b}_{n}$$
So

$$\left(\left[\right. r \mathbf{u} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = \left[\right. r c_{1} \vdots r c_{n} \left]\right. = r \left[\right. c_{1} \vdots c_{n} \left]\right. = r \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u} \left]\right.\right)_{B}$$

Thus the coordinate mapping also preserves scalar multiplication and hence is a linear transformation. See Exercises 27 and 28 for verification that the coordinate mapping is one-to-one and maps $$V$$ onto $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .

The linearity of the coordinate mapping extends to linear combinations, just as in Section 1.8. If $$\mathbf{u}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ are in $$V$$ and if $$c_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} c_{p}$$ are scalars, then

$$\left(\left[\right. c_{1} \mathbf{u}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \mathbf{u}_{p} \left]\right.\right)_{B} = c_{1} \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u}_{1} \left]\right.\right)_{B} + \hdots + c_{p} \left(\left[\right. \mathbf{u}_{p} \left]\right.\right)_{B}$$
In words, (5) says that the $$B \text{-coordinate}$$ vector of a linear combination of $$\mathbf{u}_{1}, \text{…} \text{,} \mathbf{u}_{p}$$ is the same linear combination of their coordinate vectors.

The coordinate mapping in Theorem 9 is an important example of an isomorphism from $$V$$ onto $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . In general, a one-to-one linear transformation from a vector space $$V$$ onto a vector space $$W$$ is called an isomorphism from $$V$$ onto $$W$$ (iso from the Greek for “the same,” and morph from the Greek for “form” or “structure”). The notation and terminology for $$V$$ and $$W$$ may differ, but the two spaces are indistinguishable as vector spaces. Every vector space calculation in $$V$$ is accurately reproduced in $$W$$ , and vice versa. In particular, any real vector space with a basis of $$n$$ vectors is indistinguishable from $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . See Exercises 29 and 30.

note.paragraph: STUDY GUIDE offers additional resources about isomorphic vector spaces.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$B$$ be the standard basis of the space $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ of polynomials; that is, let $$B = \left\{ 1 \text{,} t \text{,} t^{2} \text{,} t^{3} \right\}$$ . A typical element $$\mathbf{p}$$ of $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ has the form
$$\mathbf{p} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = a_{0} + a_{1} t + a_{2} t^{2} + a_{3} t^{3}$$
Since $$\mathbf{p}$$ is already displayed as a linear combination of the standard basis vectors, we conclude that
$$\left[\right. \mathbf{p} \left]\right._{B} = \left[\right. a_{0} a_{1} a_{2} a_{3} \left]\right.$$

Thus the coordinate mapping $$\mathbf{p}\mapsto\left\lbrack {\mathbf{p}} \right\rbrack_{B}$$ is an isomorphism from $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ onto $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ . All vector space operations in $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ correspond to operations in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ .

section.paragraph: If we think of $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ as displays on two computer screens that are connected via the coordinate mapping, then every vector space operation in $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ on one screen is exactly duplicated by a corresponding vector operation in $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ on the other screen. The vectors on the $${\mathbb{P}}_{3}$$ screen look different from those on the $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ screen, but they “act” as vectors in exactly the same way. See Figure 6.

image.alt: A tablet on the left shows a polynomial expression, while a laptop screen on the right shows a column matrix with entries a subscript 0, a subscript 1, a subscript 2, and a subscript 3.

figure.caption: Figure 6 The space ℙ3 is isomorphic to ℝ4﻿

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Use coordinate vectors to verify that the polynomials $$1 + 2t^{2}$$ , $$4 + t + 5t^{2}$$ , and $$3 + 2t$$ are linearly dependent in $${\mathbb{P}}_{2}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The coordinate mapping from Example 5 produces the coordinate vectors $$(1 \text{,} 0 \text{,} 2)$$ , $$(4 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 5)$$ , and $$(3 \text{,} 2 \text{,} 0)$$ , respectively. Writing these vectors as the columns of a matrix $$A$$ , we can determine their independence by row reducing the augmented matrix for $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ :

The columns of $$A$$ are linearly dependent, so the corresponding polynomials are linearly dependent. In fact, it is easy to check that column $$3$$ of $$A$$ is $$2$$ times column $$2$$ minus $$5$$ times column $$1$$ . The corresponding relation for the polynomials is
$$3 + 2 t = 2 \left(\right. 4 + t + 5 t^{2} \left.\right) - 5 \left(\right. 1 + 2 t^{2} \left.\right)$$

section.paragraph: The final example concerns a plane in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ that is isomorphic to $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Let
$$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \left[\right. 3 6 2 \left]\right. , \mathbf{v}_{2} = \left[\right. - 1 0 1 \left]\right. , \mathbf{x} = \left[\right. 3 12 7 \left]\right. ,$$

and $$B = \{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ . Then $$B$$ is a basis for $$H = \text{Span} \{\mathbf{v}_{1} \text{,} \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$$ . Determine if $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H$$ , and if it is, find the coordinate vector of $$\mathbf{x}$$ relative to $$B$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{x}$$ is in $$H$$ , then the following vector equation is consistent:
$$c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 6 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} - 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 12 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$
The scalars $$c_{1}$$ and $$c_{2}$$ , if they exist, are the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of $$\mathbf{x}$$ . Using row operations, we obtain
$$\begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 1 & 3 \\ 6 & 0 & 1 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

Thus $$c_{1} = 2$$ , $$c_{2} = 3$$ , and $$\left\lbrack \mathbf{x} \right\rbrack_{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ . The coordinate system on $$H$$ determined by $$B$$ is shown in Figure 7.

image.alt: A figure shows a rectangular plane on a three-dimensional coordinate plane.

figure.caption: Figure 7 A coordinate system on a plane H in ℝ3

section.paragraph: If a different basis for $$H$$ were chosen, would the associated coordinate system also make $$H$$ isomorphic to $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ ? Surely, this must be true. We shall prove it in the next section.
